identity.title: Theoretical Limitations of Ensembles in the Age of Overparameterization

problem.claim: The paper asks why overparameterized neural-network ensembles may lack the generalization advantage associated with classic ensembles.

gap.claim: Existing underparameterized-ensemble intuitions do not explain how modern overparameterized ensembles differ from classic counterparts.

contributions.claim: Develops a theory of overparameterized ensembles using random-feature regressors.

Proves that infinite overparameterized random-feature ensembles are pointwise equivalent to infinite-width single regressors, while finite ensembles rapidly approach single models with the same parameter budget.
Characterizes ensemble-member predictive variance as reflecting expected capacity-increase effects rather than conventional uncertainty.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish modern overparameterized ensembles from classic underparameterized ensembles through an RF-regressor theory showing near-equivalence to suitably large single models.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report exact equivalence for ridgeless models and approximate equivalence for small ridge penalties.
The authors report that overparameterized ensembles and single large models therefore exhibit nearly identical generalization.
The authors report that ensemble predictive variance quantifies expected capacity effects, not conventional uncertainty.

narrative_sequence.summary: Classic ensembles are described as generalizing better than individual component models, whereas recent studies report no inherent advantage for modern overparameterized neural-network ensembles.
The paper uses random-feature regressors to clarify the distinction between underparameterized and overparameterized ensembles.
Under minimal assumptions, infinite overparameterized ensembles become pointwise equivalent to infinite-width single models, and finite ensembles rapidly converge to same-budget single models.
The equivalence is exact without ridge and approximate for small ridge; the reported consequence is nearly identical generalization and a challenge to transferred ensemble intuitions.
Predictive variance among members is characterized as a capacity-effect measure rather than conventional uncertainty.

source_observation.claim: The abstract states the model-regime conditions and regularization qualification alongside the equivalence result.

lessons.interpretation: A theoretical claim becomes more informative when its scope and approximation conditions are attached directly to the result.
lessons.application: State any ensemble-versus-single-model comparison together with parameterization regime, width, ridge setting, and whether the claim is exact or approximate.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the result is deliberately regime-agnostic or when those conditions are unavailable.

source_observation.claim: The paper separates predictive variance from conventional uncertainty and assigns it a capacity-related interpretation.

lessons.interpretation: Naming what a statistic measures—and what it does not—can prevent an attractive but unsupported interpretation.
lessons.application: When introducing an uncertainty-like quantity, explicitly identify its reported target and distinguish it from competing meanings.
lessons.exception: Do not impose this distinction when the quantity has been independently validated for the intended uncertainty notion.

unknowns: The abstract does not report datasets, numerical results, or experimental details.
It does not establish whether the RF theory quantitatively predicts behavior for deep neural-network ensembles.
The assumptions and convergence rates behind the theoretical claims are not specified in the abstract.
